Eating Chinese America

Chinese California,
Mapped Through
the Oldest Restaurants

More than 4,000 Chinese restaurants operate in California today. Each dot is a restaurant still in business.

Their distribution traces 170 years of migration, labor, exclusion, reinvention, and settlement.

Scroll to follow the route

The Route

As we chase the next "oldest," it helps to zoom out.

These still-open restaurants matter because they turn history into a route people can actually follow.

Mining camps. Railroad towns. Delta levees. Farm communities. Fishing ports. Suburban plazas.

Gold Rush Foothills, 1848–1870s

California's earliest Chinese communities formed beside mining camps and railroad worksites.

Foothill Chinatowns once held stores, boarding houses, temples, laundries, and herbal shops. In many towns, almost nothing remains. Sometimes one building carries the memory of an entire community.

The Chew Kee Store in Fiddletown. The Joss House in Auburn.

Most restaurants in the foothills today serve Mandarin or Sichuan. The early Cantonese miners would not have recognized the menu.

Lost · Gold Rush Foothills · Auburn

Shanghai Bar & Restaurant
1896 — 2005

289 Washington St, Auburn

Almost all old Auburnites have a story about shenanigans at the Shanghai — bootlegging during Prohibition, illegal gambling, and the like. Charlie Yue founded it in 1896; his grandsons ran it no less memorably. Live music every day: blues, jazz, country, rock.

"Liquor in the front, poker in the rear, and good eatin on the side."

Auburn Journal, Nov. 25, 1982

Delta Communities, 1860s–1920s

Chinese laborers built the levees that reshaped the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta into farmland.

River towns grew around agricultural work and seasonal migration. Restaurants stood beside groceries, association halls, temples, and boarding houses.

Locke was built by Chinese residents, for Chinese residents. One of the last rural Chinese American landscapes still standing.

Lost · Sacramento Delta · Locke

Locke Garden Restaurant
1912 — 2023

River Road, Locke

Its restaurant closed in 2023. The building needed safety upgrades. No one could cover the cost.

A reminder that places do not vanish only through forgetting. Sometimes buildings simply become too expensive to keep standing.

River News Herald and Isleton Journal, Jun. 9, 1982 · Library of Congress, HABS

Lost · Sacramento Valley · Woodland

Chicago Cafe
1903 — 2025

411 Main Street, Woodland

Chicago Cafe may have been the oldest continuously operating Chinese restaurant in California. It was also the last remnant of Woodland's Chinatown and the final business run by the Fong family.

In 2025, Nancy and Paul Fong closed the doors and retired.

A closer look at the historic restaurant that made Woodland a destination, and the family that kept it alive for over a century.

Watch the full documentary →

Photo: L06-012, UC Davis Special Collections

Central Valley Towns, 1870s–1950s

Chinese restaurants spread through railroad stops and agricultural towns across the Central Valley.

Some became local institutions long before anyone called them historic. A few are still open in Fresno, Stockton, and Bakersfield.

Hanford adds another layer: a rural town that once had a Chinese-French fusion restaurant winning awards from the American Academy of Chefs. Wealthy patrons flew in for the escargot, made with cashew butter and ginger.

Lost · Central Valley · Hanford

Chinese Pagoda & Imperial Dynasty
1883 — 2005

Hanford, Kings County

Hanford is a long way from anywhere. A rural Central Valley town that once had a Chinese-French fusion restaurant winning awards from the American Academy of Chefs and the Black Hat Chefs Society.

Wealthy patrons flew in for the escargot, made with cashew butter and ginger. The wine cellar was converted from an old opium den.

The Sentinel, 2024

Central Coast Corridor, 1870s–1940s

Along the Central Coast, Chinese restaurant history appears in fragments.

A dining room. A roadside sign. A fishing village. A Chinatown that no longer exists.

The region was shaped by farming, fishing, seasonal labor, and tourism. In many towns, the restaurants are the last visible trace.

Lost · Central Coast · Salinas

Republic Cafe
1937 — 1988

39 Soledad Street, Salinas

John Steinbeck was born near Salinas' Chinatown. The Chinatown also contained a Japantown and a Filipinotown. The Republic Cafe held community events for all of them.

Courtesy noehill.com

Southern California Suburbs, 1940s–Present

After 1965, Chinese settlement expanded beyond historic Chinatowns into the San Gabriel Valley.

Cities like Monterey Park, Alhambra, and Arcadia mark a different kind of Chinese California — not Gold Rush or railroad California, but the geography of post-1965 immigration and suburbanization.

Lost · Los Angeles

Man Jen Low
1878 — 1985

475 Gin Ling Way, New Chinatown, Los Angeles

Man Jen Low opened in Old Chinatown. When the neighborhood was demolished for Union Station in 1938, it moved to New Chinatown. Part Hollywood landmark, part banquet hall, part tourist destination.

"We have a lot of celebrities, all kind of people coming..."David Lee and Jennie Lee Wong, grandchildren of founder Wu Hoi, 1979

USC Libraries / California Historical Society, CHS-35164

Still Here

California's oldest surviving Chinese restaurants, from the redwood coast to Los Angeles.

Each has outlasted earthquakes, displacement, redevelopment, recessions, and a pandemic.
